Today, my sister came downstairs and thought my furry associate, Ginger, and I working together was a wholesome scene. But the picture she took captured more than just that. I never got to meet my mom's mom. She passed away from breast cancer. My mom has both first-degree and second-degree relatives who have battled or died from breast cancer. So you'd think getting coverage for hereditary cancer genetic testing would be straightforward. It wasn't. Today, I spent over four hours trying to push through an appeal for a denial my mom received after that testing. And while I'm glad Ginger felt relaxed, the chaos happening on the phone made me feel quite the opposite. I was bounced between the ordering practice, the testing center, a prior authorization management company, and the insurance company, each one pointing me somewhere else. My mom had been told an appeal letter was submitted. It wasn't. When I read through the denial, I realized the name of the test, the procedure codes, the medical necessity rationale, and the family history documentation had never been submitted properly. And as frustrating as that is, the more I learn about this system, the more I see it isn't always negligence. It's the result of a broken prior authorization and appeals workflow. Nothing is easy. Nothing is straightforward. Everything is costly. In the past month, Loryn Canty and I have spoken with medical assistants, administrators, and providers who are completely burnt out from fighting denials and appeals. That burden doesn't stop with insurers or front offices. Eventually it reaches the patient. Today, that patient was my mom. She’s a hardworking elementary school teacher and a single mom who has spent every second outside of work supporting my sister and me. She got this testing to understand her own inherited cancer risk, and what it could mean for her daughters. She shouldn't have to spend hours fighting for coverage she already pays for. No patient should. Sitting there, dialing number after number, fighting through robots on the phone, piecing together a denial that should have been handled months ago, I remembered exactly why I started building Praxigen . Healthcare should be accessible without forcing patients, physicians, and staff to carry the weight of a broken system. Tonight, I used Praxigen to write my mom's appeal letter. Now we wait... and keep on building for the millions more who are facing it too. #PriorAuthorization #HealthTech #PatientAdvocacy #HealthcareInnovation #Praxigen 🩵 ...more ...more

I am excited to share that I will be fulfilling a lifelong dream and heading to Palo Alto next month to pursue my MBA at the Stanford Graduate School of Business! I am incredibly grateful for the people who have helped me get here — especially my family, friends, mentors, colleagues, and clients who have supported me, challenged me, and taught me so much along the way. My three years at McKinsey have been an incredibly formative part of my life. I have had the opportunity to work with amazing people, take on challenges I never expected, and learn a great deal about leadership and myself. I am especially grateful to McKinsey and my sponsors for supporting me as I take this next step, and I look forward to staying close to the people that have made these years so meaningful. I cannot wait to learn and grow alongside the GSB community over the next two years. See you on the Farm!

Anker and I went through Y Combinator in the summer of 2024. It's one of the best things we've ever done, and I'd recommend it to any early-stage founder. Growing up in Denmark, we had only ever read about Silicon Valley. It felt like a mystical place where people built things we couldn't. YC taught us a lot, but the most important lesson was that we can build something big if we work hard (and smart) enough. That's what gave us the confidence to pivot into AI customer support in the middle of the batch, even though the market was already crowded. Two years (and a lot of late nights) later, Parahelp agents have resolved millions of customer issues for the world’s fastest-growing companies like Cursor and Replit . We'll both be at the YC Internship Expo this Saturday. If you want to help build Parahelp into the leading AI support platform, come talk to us: https://yc.link/r/DcTHZS3h

I was the youngest employee at Sana when I joined, at Parahelp I’m the oldest. I just turned 26… There are actually more similarities between the two, then differences - other than the fact that both are Scandinavian. Extreme talent. When I joined Sana, I was so impressed by the team and constantly felt like an imposter. Sana managed to hire some of the most amazing people, including Anton Osika - who unfortunately left before I joined. Parahelp managed to do that too: Mads , Anker and the rest of the team are top notch. The main difference is that we are fully AI enabled at Parahelp, allowing us to do far more with less headcount. Everything is automated and efficient - a truly impressive setup. Customer obsession. I’ve rarely seen companies care as much as they do. At Sana we would call our customers partners, since that’s how we truly viewed them. The Impact (Engagement) team would go above and beyond to make a customer win and pulled out some all nighters once in a while - myself included. In hindsight, our lives would have been significantly easier if we would have used Parahelp from the start. It would have saved us countless of hours… That same care is very visible at Parahelp. No matter if you’re a member of the Customer Acceleration team or not, everyone takes initiatives to respond to our customers within seconds. Even our founders - sometime I think they’re just AI bots given how quick they spot things… Incredible products. I remember the first time I touched Sana. It felt like a magical experience, it made me happy and brought me joy. Same thing with Parahelp. I’m so impressed by the intelligence of our agents and how capable it is. Yesterday I built an entire new integration for a customer with the agent. This would normally have taken me a couple of days, with Parahelp I did it in two hours! I feel extremely lucky to have been part of both! My footprint at Sana was left, now it’s time to do the same at Parahelp. 🚀

I just finished my summer internship as a Product Manager at Microsoft , and I wanted to take a moment to reflect on what I learned over the last three months. I worked on the Word Copilot team, specifically focused on agent evaluations. While I had experience using agents, this internship enabled me to build and evaluate agents at scale. My biggest takeaway was how much evaluation infrastructure shapes the product itself. Working through user-intent classification, data drift, and designing evals that actually reflected real usage made it clear that whatever you choose to measure becomes what the team optimizes for. Evals are closer to a product spec than a quality gate. I also learned how much iteration goes into improving AI products. Running experiments and navigating tradeoffs between quality, latency, and cost reinforced the importance of pairing technical understanding with strong product judgment. Most importantly, customer obsession remained the guiding principle. With agents, it’s easy to chase better metrics or greater capability, but what matters is whether we’re ultimately driving better outcomes for customers. Grateful to Caroline Brown , Maritza Cartaya , and the many others who made these three months such a meaningful experience. I'm excited to take these lessons with me into my next chapter!
